messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Re: Using dBref in meanpec and spec
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Re: Using dBref in meanpec and spec
messages.body_plain:
Dear Mike,

Thanks for this. This non-normalization option was actually on my TODO
list for the next release. I will also add the option for spec() and
meanspec() functions.

Jerome

Mike Crowe <mpc...@gmail.com> a �crit�:

>
>
> On Friday, July 27, 2012 9:37:14 AM UTC-5, Mike Crowe wrote:
>>
>> Greetings!
>> I am using your great package to look at the self noise of an
>> accelerometer and have run into a problem.   Specificallly when I execute
>>
>> meanspec(raw_data$Ax, f=(f*1000), wl=win_len, dB="max0",
>> dBref=(sens*bw_sqrt) , flab="Frequency(Hz)", alab="Noise dBuG/Hz^0.5")
>>
>> I get results that are not consistent.  I reviewd the source code in
>> seewave.r and found that the spectral result is being normalized to the max
>> bin
>> e.g. y3<-y2/max(y2)
>>
>> If something like
>> if(is.null(dBref)) y3<-y2/max(y2)
>> else y3<-y2
>> were to be implemented when using dBref, then absolute calibrations could
>> be performed.
>>
>> I edited the source code to try this out, but then my inexperience with
>> building packages stopped me.  When I tried to execute
>> R CMD build seewave
>>
>> the following error occurred

>> Error: processing vignette ?seewave_IO.rnw? failed with diagnostics:
>>  chunk 14
>> Error in library(sound) : there is no package called ?sound?

>>
>> How do I go about getting a changes like this implemented (locally and in
>> the main branch)?
>>
>> Thanks
>> Mike
>>
>
> So I fixed my petty compile problems by installing the package sound
> (appears to only be required for compile?).  And made the above
> modifications.  I also ran into an issue with the stft function when norm
> is set to false, the function still normalized the return values, I
> replaced the offending function with a window length normalization
> #  else {z<-z2/max(z2)}
>   else {z<-z2/(wl/2)}
> which provides the expected response.
> Cheers
> Mike
>

messages.subject: Re: [seewave] Detecting Gerygone in the secondary forest
messages.subject_clean: [seewave] Detecting Gerygone in the secondary forest
messages.body_plain:
Hi Kevin,

Your issue seems to be due to the normalisation applied by spectro()
on the spectroram matrix as discussed by Mike Crowe. An option will be
available in the next release of seewave to turn off this normalisation.

To be honest, I am not sure seewave will be the best tool for
automatic ID. I guess Songscope will do it better and, above all, much
faster.

Thanks for using seewave,

Best

Jerome

Kevin Darras <kevind...@gmail.com> a �crit�:

> Hello everyone,
> First off, thanks for the great R package!
>
> I have done some test recordings with Song Meters in secondary forest in
> Sumatra. Now I am comparing the performance and usefulness of Song Scope to
> Seewave for our research. I have been working on it for a while, but I
> stumble upon a problem:
>
> I want to compare a reference call of 3 seconds to a 100s recording which I

> know contains 5 other calls of the bird *Gerygone sulphurea*.
>
> I kept only frequencies between 3500 and 5000 Hz. I use *covspectro* (*
> corenv* never ended) to compare the reference call:
>
> to successive parts of the 100s recording, extracted with *cutw*. The

> problem is, the extracted parts look like that:
>

> although in the original spectogram, the parts are white and relatively
> silent, only containing background noise. I guess the spectrograms use red
> for the highest amplitude (even if it is low) and color the other sounds
> relative to the loudest sound.
> However, the correlations between my reference call and those background
> noise parts are highly significant (coef>90%) and the time offset is always
> 0. There is no way to distinguish really significant correlations (between
> two real calls) from unsignificant ones (between reference call and
> background noise). Is there a way to disable the amplitude autoscaling such
> that comparisons with background noise do not turn out so significant?
> I attach my code here:
>
>> rm(list = ls())
>> setwd("D:/Burung")
>> library(seewave)
>> library(tuneR)
>> freq=22050
>> song<-readWave("original_part.wav")
>>
>> songf<-resamp(song,f=44100,g=freq,output="Wave")
>> songf<-ffilter(songf,from=3500,to=5000,output="Wave")
>>
>> reff<-cutw(songf,from=10.75,to=13.75,plot=FALSE,output="Wave")
>>
>> RESU=NULL
>> dura=trunc(length(songf)/freq)
>> refd=trunc(length(reff)/freq)
>> bins<-seq(from=1,to=trunc(dura),by=refd/2)
>> pb <- txtProgressBar(min=0,max=max(bins),style=3)
>>
>> for (i in bins){
>>   scan<-cutw(songf,from=i,to=i+refd,output="Wave")
>>   resu<-covspectro(reff,scan,f=freq,n=15,plot=FALSE)
>>   RESU<-cbind(RESU,resu)
>>   Sys.sleep(0.1)
>>   setTxtProgressBar(pb,i)
>> }
>> close(pb)
>>
> Am I doing a mistake?

> I would like to add that it would be handy if *covspectro* could compare

> time waves of different lengths.
> Greetings from Sumatra
>
